title: Accounting for Partnership: Fundamentals
description: Class 12 Accountancy: partnership meaning and deed, provisions of the Partnership Act, Profit & Loss Appropriation Account, fixed vs fluctuating capital accounts, and interest on capital and drawings with solved examples.

topics.title: Partnership, the Deed and the Provisions of the Act
topics.concept:
A partnership is the relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all (Indian Partnership Act, 1932). The persons are individually called partners and collectively a firm.

Its essential features: (i) two or more persons; (ii) an agreement; (iii) a lawful business; (iv) sharing of profits; and (v) mutual agency (each partner is both an agent and a principal — the act of one binds all). The maximum number of partners is 50 (Companies Act / Rules).

The partnership deed is the written agreement among the partners. It usually states the name of the firm, the capital of each partner, the profit-sharing ratio, interest on capital and drawings, partners' salary/commission, and how disputes are settled. A deed is not compulsory but is highly desirable, because it prevents disputes.

When there is no deed, or the deed is silent on a point, the provisions of the Partnership Act apply:

MatterRule in the absence of a deed
Profit-sharing ratioEqual, whatever the capitals
Interest on capitalNot allowed
Interest on drawingsNot charged
Salary/commission to a partnerNot allowed
Interest on a partner's loan to the firm6% p.a. (a charge, allowed even in loss)

These default rules are a favourite exam topic. Note especially that profits are shared equally (not in the capital ratio) and that a partner's loan still earns 6% even when the firm makes a loss.

examples.problem: Example 1: A and B are partners with no deed. A contributed Rs 80,000 and B Rs 40,000. In what ratio do they share profits?
examples.solution:
No deed → equal.

  • Without a deed, profits are shared equally, regardless of capital.
examples.answer: Equally (1:1) — the unequal capitals do not matter when there is no deed.

examples.problem: Example 2: A partner gave the firm a loan of Rs 1,00,000. The deed is silent on interest. How much interest is due?
examples.solution:
Loan rule applies.

  • In the absence of a deed, a partner's loan earns 6% p.a.
  • 6% of 1,00,000 = Rs 6,000 per year.
examples.answer: Rs 6,000 per year (interest on a partner's loan is 6% p.a. even without a deed).

examples.problem: Example 3: What is meant by 'mutual agency' in a partnership?
examples.solution:
Agent and principal.

  • Each partner is both an agent (can bind the firm) and a principal (bound by others' acts).
examples.answer: Each partner is both an agent and a principal — the act of one partner in business binds all the others.

recap:
• Partnership: 2+ persons, agreement, lawful business, profit-sharing, mutual agency; max 50 partners.
  • Deed = written agreement (ratio, capital, interest, salary). Desirable, not compulsory.
  • No deed → Act applies: profits equal; no interest on capital/drawings; no salary; partner's loan 6% p.a.

quiz.q: With no partnership deed, profits are shared:
quiz.explanation: In the absence of a deed, profits are shared equally.

quiz.q: Interest on a partner's loan, when the deed is silent, is:
quiz.explanation: A partner's loan earns 6% p.a. even without a deed.

topics.title: Profit & Loss Appropriation Account
topics.concept:
In a sole proprietorship, net profit simply goes to the owner. In a partnership it must be distributed among the partners after various adjustments. This distribution is shown in a special account called the Profit & Loss Appropriation Account — an extension of the P&L Account, prepared after net profit is found.

The distinction to master: a charge against profit is deducted to find net profit (e.g. rent, interest on a partner's loan); an appropriation of profit is a distribution of net profit (interest on capital, partner's salary, transfer to reserve). Charges go in the P&L Account; appropriations go in the P&L Appropriation Account.

Dr — P&L Appropriation A/c — Cr 
To Interest on CapitalBy Net Profit b/d (from P&L)
To Partner's Salary / CommissionBy Interest on Drawings
To Reserve (transfer) 
To Profit transferred to Partners' Capital A/cs (in PSR) 

The order is: start with net profit (credit), add interest on drawings (credit), then deduct interest on capital, salary/commission and reserve; the balance left is the divisible profit, shared among partners in their profit-sharing ratio. For example, net profit Rs 1,00,000; interest on capital Rs 12,000; A's salary Rs 18,000; the divisible profit = 1,00,000 − 12,000 − 18,000 = Rs 70,000, shared in the PSR. If the appropriations exceed available profit, they are usually allowed only in the ratio of the amounts due (unless the deed says they are a charge).

examples.problem: Example 1: Distinguish a charge against profit from an appropriation of profit.
examples.solution:
Find vs distribute.

  • A charge is deducted to find net profit (e.g. rent, interest on partner's loan).
  • An appropriation distributes net profit (interest on capital, salary, reserve).
examples.answer: A charge is deducted to find net profit; an appropriation distributes the net profit already found.

examples.problem: Example 2: Net profit Rs 90,000; interest on capital Rs 10,000; B's salary Rs 20,000. Find the divisible profit.
examples.answer: Divisible profit = Rs 60,000 (shared in the profit-sharing ratio).

examples.problem: Example 3: Is interest on a partner's loan shown in the P&L Account or the Appropriation Account?
examples.solution:
It is a charge.

  • Interest on a partner's loan is a charge against profit.
  • So it is in the P&L Account, not the Appropriation Account.
examples.answer: In the Profit & Loss Account (it is a charge against profit, not an appropriation).

recap:
• P&L Appropriation A/c distributes net profit after appropriations.
  • Charge (find profit): rent, interest on partner's loan → P&L A/c. Appropriation (distribute): interest on capital, salary, reserve → Appropriation A/c.
  • Divisible profit = net profit + interest on drawings − interest on capital − salary − reserve; shared in PSR.

quiz.explanation: Interest on capital is an appropriation of profit.

quiz.q: The Profit & Loss Appropriation Account is prepared:
quiz.explanation: It distributes the net profit already determined by the P&L Account.

topics.title: Partners' Capital Accounts: Fixed vs Fluctuating, Interest on Capital & Drawings
topics.concept:
Each partner has a capital account. There are two methods of maintaining them.

  • Fluctuating Capital Method — one account per partner. All items (capital, interest on capital, salary, share of profit, drawings, interest on drawings) pass through it, so its balance fluctuates every year. This is the default when the deed is silent.
  • Fixed Capital Method — two accounts per partner: the Capital Account (which stays fixed, recording only capital introduced or withdrawn) and a Current Account (which records all the other items — interest, salary, profit share, drawings). The capital figure therefore stays constant.

Two key calculations recur:

Interest on Capital = Capital × Rate × Time. It is allowed only if the deed provides, and only out of profit (it is an appropriation). For example, capital Rs 2,00,000 at 6% p.a. = Rs 12,000.

Interest on Drawings = charged when the deed allows, to discourage withdrawals. If drawings are made evenly through the year, the average period is 6 months, so interest = total drawings × rate × 6/12. The product method is used when drawings of different amounts are made on different dates: multiply each drawing by the months it stayed in the business, total the products, and charge interest on the total for one month. For example, drawings of Rs 10,000 on 1 April (12 months) and Rs 10,000 on 1 October (6 months) give products 1,20,000 + 60,000 = 1,80,000; interest at 6% = 1,80,000 × 6% × 1/12 = Rs 900.

Mastering these — the appropriation account and the capital accounts — is the foundation for everything else in partnership: goodwill, admission, retirement and dissolution all build on them.

examples.problem: Example 1: Under the fixed capital method, how many accounts does each partner have, and what are they?
examples.solution:
Two accounts.

  • A Capital Account (fixed) and a Current Account (for all other items).
examples.answer: Two — a fixed Capital Account and a Current Account.

examples.problem: Example 2: A's capital is Rs 3,00,000; interest on capital is 8% p.a. Find the interest.
Example 3: A partner draws Rs 6,000 evenly each month all year; interest on drawings is 10% p.a. Find the interest using the average period.
examples.solution:
Total drawings × rate × 6/12.

  • Total drawings = 6,000 × 12 = 72,000.
  • Average period = 6 months → interest = 72,000 × 10% × 6/12 = 3,600.

recap:
• Fluctuating capital = one account (default); Fixed = Capital (fixed) + Current account.
  • Interest on capital = Capital × Rate × Time (an appropriation, only from profit).
  • Interest on drawings: even drawings → average period 6 months; varying drawings → product method.

quiz.explanation: When the deed is silent, capital accounts are fluctuating.

quiz.q: Under the fixed capital method, a partner's salary is credited to the:
quiz.explanation: All items other than capital go to the Current Account under the fixed method.

questions.explanation: Fluctuating capital is the default.

questions.q: A and B contributed capitals of 3,00,000 and 1,00,000 with no deed. The firm earned 80,000. A claims profit in the capital ratio 3:1. He is:
options: Wrong — without a deed profit is shared equally (40,000 each)
questions.explanation: In the absence of a deed the Act overrides capital — profits are equal, so 40,000 each.

questions.q: A partner's loan of 2,00,000 (deed silent on interest) in a year the firm made a LOSS. The interest:
options: Is still allowed at 6% as a charge
Is not allowed in a loss
questions.explanation: Interest on a partner's loan is a charge against profit and is allowed even when the firm makes a loss.

questions.q: Net profit before appropriations is 50,000. Interest on capital due is 40,000 and salary due is 30,000 (total 70,000, deed says these are appropriations). They are allowed:
options: In the ratio 40:30, limited to the 50,000 available
questions.explanation: When profit is insufficient and items are appropriations, they are distributed in the ratio of amounts due (4:3) up to the available profit.

questions.q: A draws 12,000 at the END of every quarter; interest on drawings 10% p.a. Using the product method the average period is:
questions.explanation: Quarter-end drawings stay 9,6,3,0 months → average (9+6+3+0)/4 = 4.5 months.

questions.q: Under the FIXED capital method, in which account is a partner's share of profit recorded?
questions.explanation: Only capital introduced/withdrawn touches the fixed Capital Account; profit goes to the Current Account.

questions.q: A guarantee that a partner's share will be at least 25,000 is met by net profit 60,000 shared equally between A, B, C, with C guaranteed. C's actual share and the deficiency are:
options: C's 20,000, deficiency 5,000 borne by A and B
questions.explanation: Equal share = 20,000; the 5,000 shortfall to reach the 25,000 guarantee is borne by the other partners.

questions.q: Why is interest on capital NOT allowed in a year of loss (when it is an appropriation)?
options: Appropriations are made only out of available profit
questions.explanation: Being an appropriation, interest on capital can only be provided if there is profit to distribute.

questions.q: A partner is entitled to a commission of 10% of net profit AFTER charging such commission. If profit before commission is 1,10,000, the commission is:
questions.explanation: Commission = 1,10,000 × 10/110 = 10,000 (so profit after = 1,00,000, 10% of which is 10,000).

questions.q: The fluctuating capital method differs from the fixed method in that the capital balance:
options: Changes every year as all items pass through it
questions.explanation: With a single account, profit, interest, salary and drawings all alter the balance each year.
